interviewQuestions.question: Is the language {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 0} context-free?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start with intuition before reaching for a formal tool: a pushdown automaton has exactly one stack, and matching `aⁿbⁿ` is easy with one stack — push on `a`, pop on `b`. But I now need a *second* independent count (`c`) to also equal `n`, and one stack can't check two separate counts at once.

To make that rigorous, I'd apply the **pumping lemma for context-free languages**: assume the language is context-free, pick a long enough string `aᵖbᵖcᵖ`, and show that any valid way to split and "pump" a middle section either breaks the equal-count property or breaks the ordering (a's-then-b's-then-c's) — every case leads to a string no longer in the language, a contradiction.

So I'd conclude it is **not** context-free — it needs at least a context-sensitive grammar, since you're checking three counts against each other, not two.

**Testing:** whether you can connect a computational-model argument (one stack, two things to check) to a real proof technique (pumping lemma), not just assert an answer from memory.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Proving a^n b^n c^n isn't context-free

interviewQuestions.question: What does it mean for a grammar to be ambiguous, and why does an ambiguous grammar cause real problems for a parser, not just a theoretical inconvenience?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A grammar is ambiguous if some string in the language it defines has **two or more distinct parse trees** — two genuinely different derivations, not just two different sequences of the same rule applications. Since a parse tree usually determines meaning (an AST feeds directly into evaluation or code generation), ambiguity means the grammar alone doesn't determine what a valid input actually means.

The canonical example is the dangling-else problem: `if a then if b then s1 else s2` is ambiguous in a naive grammar for if-then-else, because the `else` could attach to either the inner or outer `if`, producing two different parse trees with two different runtime behaviors depending on which `if` actually executes `s2`. A parser generator (yacc, ANTLR) will either flag this as a grammar conflict (a shift-reduce conflict, in LALR terms) or silently resolve it via a default rule — most commonly 'attach else to the nearest unmatched if' — which is precisely why every language with this construct has an explicit, documented rule for it rather than leaving it to the reader's intuition.

The engineering consequence: an ambiguous grammar either needs to be rewritten to be unambiguous (adding explicit disambiguating rules, like requiring `endif` or mandatory braces) or the parser generator's default conflict-resolution behavior needs to be understood and accepted deliberately — silently trusting a parser generator's default resolution without knowing it exists is a real, recurring source of subtle language-design bugs.

**Testing:** whether you can define ambiguity precisely (multiple parse trees, not multiple derivation sequences) and connect it to a concrete, well-known real-world case (dangling else) rather than treating it as an abstract grammar-theory concern.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Grammar ambiguity

interviewQuestions.question: Why can't a naive recursive-descent parser handle every context-free grammar, and what has to change about the grammar to make it work?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Recursive-descent parsing writes one function per nonterminal and decides which production to apply by looking at the next token(s) — it needs to make that choice without backtracking (in the efficient, standard form) to stay linear-time. That requirement is exactly what **LL(k)** grammars formalize: a grammar is LL(1) if, for every nonterminal, seeing just one lookahead token is always enough to determine which production applies unambiguously.

Two grammar shapes break this and need rewriting before recursive descent works cleanly. **Left recursion** (`A → Aα`) sends a naive recursive-descent function straight into infinite recursion, since the function for `A` immediately calls itself again before consuming any input — the fix is rewriting the recursive rule into an equivalent iterative loop. **Common prefixes across alternatives** of the same nonterminal (`A → αβ | αγ`) mean one token of lookahead can't tell which alternative to commit to — the fix is **left-factoring**: pull the shared prefix `α` out into its own rule so the choice point moves to where the tokens actually diverge.

The broader point this illustrates: context-free grammars as a *class* are more expressive than what any single parsing algorithm can handle efficiently — LL parsers handle a strict subset (LL grammars), LR parsers (used by yacc/bison) handle a different, larger subset (LR grammars) using a stack and lookahead differently, and some genuinely context-free languages need a general (and slower) CYK or Earley parser because they're not expressible in either restricted form at all.

**Testing:** whether you can name the two concrete grammar problems that break recursive descent (left recursion, common prefixes) and their standard fixes, rather than vaguely saying 'some grammars don't work with some parsers.'
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Parsing in practice

interviewQuestions.question:
Why can't a pure context-free grammar validate that XML/HTML tags are properly matched by name, like `
...
`, not just properly nested?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown: Balanced nesting alone — every open tag eventually closes, in the right order — is exactly the classic context-free pattern (it's the same structure as balanced parentheses, matchable with one stack: push on open, pop on close). But **matching by name** requires the popped tag's *name* to equal the pushed tag's name, which means the stack isn't just tracking depth, it's tracking an unbounded amount of *content* (the actual tag names seen) that later has to be compared for equality — and a context-free grammar's productions can't express 'whatever string appeared here earlier must reappear identically there,' because a CFG's rules are purely structural/positional, with no mechanism to carry an arbitrary remembered value forward and compare it later. This is provably not context-free by the same style of pumping-lemma argument used for `aⁿb⁻ⁿcⁿ` — the language of strings like `` but never `` requires matching identifiers across arbitrary distance, which is a context-sensitive requirement, not a context-free one. The practical fix real parsers use: an XML/HTML parser is not a pure CFG-driven parser at all — it's typically implemented as a **pushdown automaton augmented with an explicit stack of tag names** (effectively a context-free *skeleton* for nesting, plus an out-of-band equality check on tag names at each pop), which is exactly the standard technique for handling 'context-free shape, plus one extra equality constraint' languages without needing the full power (and cost) of a general context-sensitive grammar. **Testing:** whether you can identify precisely which part of the requirement exceeds context-free power (name-matching, not just nesting) and describe the real-world workaround (augmented pushdown automaton) rather than treating XML parsing as 'just CFG parsing.'
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Where context-free breaks down
